title: Why we talk to ourselves
text: Talking to yourself used to be a sign to worry {{1}}, but psychologists now see it as a sign of intelligence. 'Private speech' helps children plan actions aloud before they manage it silently, and adults {{2}} the habit under pressure. Athletes famously instruct themselves mid-performance; tennis champions have been heard {{3}} strategies between points. Studies show that self-talk works best in the second person: telling yourself 'You can do this' produces better results in difficult tasks {{4}} saying 'I can do this', perhaps because you hear it as advice from a coach. The tone matters as much as the words — {{5}} self-criticism tends to undermine performance. Researchers recommend instructional self-talk for complex {{6}} ('slowly, smooth movements') and motivational self-talk for endurance ('keep {{7}}'). Far from being a symptom, talking to yourself appears to be one of the mind's most {{8}} tools.

gaps.explanation: 'adults keep the habit' = continue it; 'continue to' would need a verb after.
'heard discussing' — the action was in progress.
